name: Ozone therapy for gums

lead: Ozone therapy for gums means using ozone gas, ozonated water or ozonated oil in the mouth to try to treat gum disease. It is the dental branch of a wider alternative medicine practice.
Public summaries of ozone therapy describe evidence for most uses as limited, and no gum-specific trial results were found in the sources reviewed here.

paras: Ozone is a strong oxidising gas that can kill microbes in the laboratory; proponents extend this to bacteria in the gums.
The FDA has stated that ozone is toxic and has no demonstrated safe medical use. Serious harms are documented mainly for injected or systemic ozone, not dental use specifically.

lead: Ozone therapy for gums refers to the use of ozone (O3), applied as a gas, ozonated water or ozonated oil, in the mouth with the aim of treating gum disease and related dental problems. It is a dental application of the broader practice of ozone therapy, which introduces ozone into the body as an alternative medicine treatment.[1]

Proponents in online dental and alternative-health circles describe ozone as a germ-killing agent that can reduce oral bacteria and support gum healing. Reviews of ozone therapy in general describe support for many proposed uses as limited,[1] and the US Food and Drug Administration has stated that ozone is a toxic gas with no demonstrated safe medical use.[1] Specific trial results for dental ozone are not covered in the pages consulted for this article.
infobox: FDA states no demonstrated safe medical use

paras: Ozone was first used in healthcare in 1856 to disinfect operating rooms and sterilise instruments. During World War I, ozone was tested on wounds at a London military hospital, where it was reported to damage both bacteria and human tissue, and antiseptic irrigation was preferred.[1]

The FDA stated in 1976, and reaffirmed in 2006, that ozone is a toxic gas without a demonstrated safe medical use, and that germicidal concentrations exceed what humans can tolerate.[1] Reported harms from systemic ozone therapy include pulmonary edema, gas embolism and other serious events; these reports concern injected or systemic routes rather than dental application specifically.[1]

No studies found. The sources consulted for this article do not summarise specific human trials of ozone for gum disease. Reviews of ozone therapy more broadly have addressed conditions such as knee osteoarthritis and herniated discs, and describe support for many other proposed uses as limited.[1]

lore.intro: Dental ozone is promoted in some alternative-health and dental-marketing contexts as a natural antibacterial option for gums.

claims.claim: Ozone kills the bacteria behind gum disease without antibiotics

timeline.event: Ozone first used in healthcare to disinfect operating rooms and instruments.[1]
FDA states ozone is a toxic gas with no demonstrated safe medical use; reaffirmed in 2006.[1]
